176.title: The city of nine gates (5.13–5.21)
176.hook: the Gita calls your body a city with nine gates, and asks who lives inside
176.howItsDone: In meditation, Hindus who practice yoga often draw attention inward from the senses, the 'gates' of Gita 5.13, and some traditions of yoga practice closing the senses one by one to rest in the self within.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two paths, and a lotus leaf that lives in the water without getting wet. Both work. Today, a city.

An old walled city at night, with nine gates in the wall. Through every gate, all day long, traffic: carts, voices, smells from the market, news, noise. And somewhere in the middle, in a quiet courtyard, someone sits perfectly at ease, watching it all come and go. Not running the gates. Not chasing the carts. Just seated. The Gita says that city is you. Count the gates on your own face and body and you'll find them. So who sits in the middle?
screen: `AN OLD CITY, NINE GATES.` → `TRAFFIC ALL DAY LONG.` → `SOMEONE SEATED IN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Verse thirteen: having let go of all actions in the mind, the one who lives in the body sits at ease in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor making anything act. The nine gates are the body's openings: two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, the mouth, and the two openings for waste. Everything the world sends you comes through one of them. The Upanishads use the same image of the body as a city with gates, and the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad plays on a word: purusha, the person, heard as the one who dwells in the city, the pura. Now the point. Who's doing all the seeing and hearing and eating? The next verses say the Lord doesn't create our sense of being the doer, or our actions, or their fruits. That's nature, doing what nature does. Knowledge is covered by ignorance, and so beings get confused. But when knowledge clears the ignorance, it lights up the highest, the way the sun lights up everything. Then a verse about how the wise see. They look with the same eye, verse eighteen says, at a learned and gentle priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a person society shuns, because the same one is seated in every city. And this stretch ends plainly: the one not attached to outside contacts finds happiness within. Busy gates. A quiet center.

segments.voice: Visit the gates one at a time: your eyes, noticing light even with them closed; your ears, the nearest sound, then the farthest; your nostrils, the cool air coming in; your mouth, the taste that's there right now. You don't have to close any gate. Just notice the traffic, and that something in the middle is noticing, and rest there.
Purusha. The person, the one who dwells in the city. The body, with its nine openings to the world, and the self seated at ease in the middle, watching.
Your line: seated within. The courtyard stays quiet, even when the gates are loud. See you tomorrow.

177.title: The sage's peace (5.22–5.29)
177.hook: every pleasure that comes from outside has a beginning and an end; chapter five ends with the one that doesn't
177.howItsDone: Hindu prayers and readings often close with 'om shanti shanti shanti', a threefold wish for peace, and some practitioners use steady, even breathing like that of Gita 5.27–28 to settle before meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, purusha: the one seated at ease in the city of nine gates. Today, the end of chapter five.

The best meal of last month: where is it now? Gone. It was wonderful, and it was over by the end of the plate. The new phone, the great weekend, the compliment that made your whole Tuesday. Each one arrived, glowed, and left, sometimes with a little ache where it had been. Nobody in the Gita says those things are bad. But the last verses of chapter five ask a sharp question about them: where's the happiness that doesn't end?
screen: `THE BEST MEAL OF LAST MONTH.` → `WHERE IS IT NOW?` → `A HAPPINESS WITH NO END?`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-two: the pleasures born of contact, of the senses touching their objects, are wombs of sorrow. They have a beginning and an end, and the wise don't take their delight in them. A womb is where something grows: every pleasure that depends on something outside carries, inside it, the sorrow of its ending. Then verse twenty-three sets a practical test. Whoever can bear the rush of desire and anger here, in this life, before leaving the body, is a yogi, a happy person. Not someone who never feels desire or anger. Someone who can bear the push of it. Verse twenty-four gives the other direction: happy within, delighting within, lit from within. That person, the text says, reaches brahma-nirvana, the stillness of Brahman. Yes, nirvana: the word is in the Gita too. Then two verses sketch a meditation, a preview of chapter six: shut out outside contacts, fix the gaze between the brows, even out the breath moving in and out of the nostrils. And the chapter's last verse names what's at the end of it all. The one who knows Krishna as the one who receives every offering, the great lord of all the worlds, and the friend of all beings, reaches peace. Shanti. That's where the sage's peace comes from: not from getting enough, but from knowing that friend.
screen: `WOMBS OF SORROW.` · `BEAR THE PUSH OF DESIRE AND ANGER.` · `LIT FROM WITHIN.` · `THE FRIEND OF ALL BEINGS.` · then, large: `SHANTI. PEACE.`

segments.voice: Verses twenty-seven and twenty-eight give a sitting, so here's a gentle version: sit tall, close your eyes or rest your gaze softly, and even out the breath, in for four, out for four, the air moving quietly through the nostrils. If a want or an irritation pushes in, don't fight it; bear it for one breath, and let it pass.
Shanti. Peace: not the pleasure that begins and ends, but the peace of the one who knows the friend of all beings.
Your line: peace. The kind that doesn't end when the plate does. Chapter five, done.

178.title: Lift yourself by yourself (6.1–6.9)
178.hook: the verse that says you are your own best friend, and your own worst enemy
178.howItsDone: Gita 6.5 is often learned by heart, and some Hindus recite it as encouragement in hard times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shanti: the sage's peace, from the friend of all beings. Today, chapter six, the chapter of meditation, and a friend much closer to home.

Listen to the voice in your head after something goes wrong. You dropped the ball at work. You snapped at someone you love. What does the voice say? For a lot of people, things they would never say to a friend. You always do this. What's wrong with you. If a stranger talked to you like that, you'd walk away. But this voice comes along everywhere. A few verses into chapter six, the Gita has two lines about exactly this voice.
screen: `SOMETHING GOES WRONG.` → `WHAT DOES THE VOICE SAY?` → `WORDS YOU'D NEVER SAY TO A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: First, Krishna clears something up. The true renouncer, verse one says, isn't the one who stops lighting the sacred fire or stops doing any work. It's the one who does what needs doing without leaning on the fruit. Verse three: for someone climbing toward yoga, action is the way up; for someone who has arrived, stillness is the way. Then verses five and six. Lift yourself by yourself; don't let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self. In Sanskrit the same word, atman, the self, comes again and again, like a mirror facing a mirror. The word for friend is bandhu: a friend, and also kin, family. Verse six explains how one self can be both. For the one who has mastered themselves, the self is a friend. For the one who hasn't, the self behaves like an enemy. Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say wait for someone to rescue you. It doesn't say you're on your own, either; later chapters speak of grace. It says the hand that lifts you starts with your own. Then a portrait of the one who has done it: steady in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, praise and blame. A lump of earth, a stone and gold look alike to them, and they're even-minded toward friend and foe, the good and the bad. Be your own friend.

segments.voice: Think of the last time the inner voice was harsh with you, and let the words come up. Now imagine a good friend heard those words said about you, and let the friend's answer come, in a warm voice. On each in-breath, lift a little, the way you'd lift someone off the floor; on each out-breath, let yourself be held.
Bandhu. Friend, kin: the self is its own bandhu. Gita six, five: the self is the friend of the self, and the enemy of the self. The lifting starts with your own hand.
Your line: your own friend. The harsh voice doesn't get the last word. Day one hundred seventy-eight.

179.title: How to sit (6.10–6.17)
179.hook: the Gita's own meditation instructions: the place, the seat, the spine, and how much to eat
179.tomorrow: The lamp in a windless place (6.18–6.28)
179.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep a clean corner or home shrine for daily sitting, often on a mat or cloth, with a straight spine and a steady gaze, following the pattern of Gita 6.10–6.17.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bandhu: lift yourself by yourself, and be your own friend. Today, where and how to sit.

Search for how to meditate and you'll get ten thousand answers. Apps, retreats, cushions that cost more than a chair. But people wrote down instructions for this a very long time ago, and chapter six of the Gita has them. Not vague ones, either. Where to sit. What to sit on. How high. How to hold your head. Where to put your eyes. And then a line that surprises people: how much to eat and sleep.
screen: `TEN THOUSAND ANSWERS.` → `WRITTEN DOWN LONG AGO.` → `WHERE, WHAT, HOW HIGH.`

segments.voice: Verse ten starts with the place. The yogi should sit alone, somewhere apart, with body and mind under control, not wanting anything, not grasping. Verse eleven: in a clean place, set a firm seat, not too high and not too low. In the old instructions it's layered: sacred kusha grass, then a deerskin, then cloth. For most people now, a folded blanket or a steady chair. Firm, clean, and yours. Verse twelve: sitting there, make the mind one-pointed, rein in thoughts and senses, and practice yoga to purify yourself. Verse thirteen, the posture: body, head and neck in a straight line, still and steady. Gaze toward the tip of the nose, the text says, and don't look around in every direction. Verse fourteen, the heart of it: calm, without fear, the mind held, sitting with the mind on Krishna, intent on him. Then the balance. Yoga, verse sixteen says, isn't for someone who eats too much, or not at all; not for someone who sleeps too much, or stays awake too long. Verse seventeen: for the one who is moderate in food and rest, in effort, in sleeping and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow. Not the heroic all-night vigil, not the lazy slump. The middle. A clean place, a steady seat, a straight spine, a quiet gaze, and a life that isn't at war with itself.
screen: `A CLEAN PLACE, A FIRM SEAT.` · `BODY, HEAD, NECK IN A LINE.` · `A STILL, INWARD GAZE.` · `NOT TOO MUCH, NOT TOO LITTLE.` · then, large: `YOGA DESTROYS SORROW.`

segments.voice: Find the steadiest seat near you, a chair or the floor, not too high and not too low, and let body, head and neck line up, as if a thread lifts the top of your head. Lower and soften the eyes toward the tip of the nose, or close them, stop looking around, and stay still. If you pray, you can hold Krishna in mind, as verse fourteen says; if not, hold the stillness itself.
Asana. The seat, and the way of sitting. The Gita's instructions: a clean place, a firm seat, body and head and neck in a line, a steady gaze, and moderation in food and sleep.
Your line: the posture, the place. Not too high, not too low, not too much. See you tomorrow.

180.title: The lamp in a windless place (6.18–6.28)
180.hook: the Gita's picture of a settled mind is a flame that doesn't flicker
180.tomorrow: "The mind is restless" — Arjuna admits it (6.29–6.36)
180.howItsDone: Hindus often light a lamp (diya) at the home shrine morning or evening, and some meditate by gazing at a steady flame; Gita 6.19's windless lamp is a classic image of the settled mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, asana: a clean place, a firm seat, a straight spine. Today, what happens once you're sitting there.

Light a small oil lamp, a diya, the kind lit at a home shrine, and set it by an open window. Watch it. The flame bends, leans, jumps, nearly goes out, flares back. Every breath of air pushes it around. Now carry it into an inner room and shut the door. The flame straightens. It stands tall and still, so still it almost looks painted. Same lamp. Same oil. The only difference is the wind. The Gita, chapter six, uses that picture for the mind.
screen: `A LAMP BY AN OPEN WINDOW.` → `SHUT THE DOOR.` → `THE FLAME STANDS STILL.`

segments.voice: Verse nineteen: as a lamp in a windless place does not flicker, that is the picture of the yogi whose mind is held, practicing union with the self. The Sanskrit is simple: dipa, the lamp; nivata, where there's no wind. Notice the lamp is still burning. A settled mind hasn't gone out. It's fully lit, just not being pushed around. Then the verses say what that stillness opens onto. Where the mind comes to rest, seeing the self by the self, a person is content in the self. They know a joy beyond the senses, grasped by understanding, and once settled there they don't move from the truth. Having gained it, they count no other gain greater. Established in it, even heavy sorrow doesn't shake them. Then a definition I like a lot, from verse twenty-three: yoga is the unhooking from union with sorrow. Yoga is often heard as joining. Here it's also an unjoining: coming apart from the grip of pain. Now the practical part. Verse twenty-five: little by little, let the mind grow still. Shanaih shanaih: slowly, slowly. And verse twenty-six gives the whole method in one sentence: wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders off, draw it back from there and bring it under the self. Not never wandering. Coming back. Every time the wind moves the flame, you shut the door again.
screen: `A LAMP THAT DOES NOT FLICKER.` · `STILL, AND FULLY LIT.` · `UNHOOKED FROM SORROW.` · `SLOWLY, SLOWLY. COME BACK.` · then, large: `THE LAMP IN A WINDLESS PLACE.`

segments.voice: Picture a small flame in the middle of your chest, or just in front of your closed eyes, and let it burn. Each time a thought blows in, notice the flame lean, then gently shut the door and watch it straighten, without being annoyed at the wind. Verse twenty-six expects it: the practice is the returning, slowly, slowly, as many times as it takes.
Dipa. Lamp. Gita six, nineteen: as a lamp in a windless place does not flicker, so is the settled mind, a flame that burns fully and doesn't flicker.
Your line: flame unwavering. Fully lit, and not pushed around. Day one hundred eighty, done.

181.title: "The mind is restless" — Arjuna admits it (6.29–6.36)
181.hook: after all the instructions, Arjuna says what everyone is thinking: this is impossible
181.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often pair abhyasa (steady practice) and vairagya (detachment) as the two supports of meditation; the Yoga Sutra names the same pair, and some practitioners return to Gita 6.34–35 when meditation feels impossible.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dipa: the lamp in a windless place, and the mind brought back, slowly, slowly. Today, someone admits how hard that is.

You sit down to be still. Ten seconds in, you're thinking about lunch. Then an email. Then a conversation from 2014 that you lost, and how you should have answered. Then lunch again. Krishna has just described the yogi who sees the self in every being, and the lamp that doesn't flicker. And Arjuna, a warrior whose whole craft is a steady aim, stops him and says, basically: I can't do this. My mind won't hold still.
screen: `TEN SECONDS IN: LUNCH.` → `THEN A CONVERSATION FROM 2014.` → `ARJUNA: I CAN'T DO THIS.`

segments.voice: First, the vision that sets Arjuna off. The yogi, verse twenty-nine says, sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self. Whoever sees Krishna everywhere and everything in him is never lost to him, and he is never lost to them. And the highest yogi, verse thirty-two, looks at another's joy or pain as if it were their own. Beautiful. And Arjuna says: this yoga of evenness you describe, I don't see how it can last, because the mind is restless. Verse thirty-four: the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, strong and stubborn. To hold it, I think, is as hard as holding the wind. Here's the surprise: Krishna doesn't argue. No doubt, he says, the mind is restless and hard to hold. Then he gives two words. By abhyasa and by vairagya, it can be held. Abhyasa: practice, doing it again and again. Vairagya: detachment, the fading of the pull, not letting every passing want drag you off. You need both. Practice alone becomes grim effort against a mind that keeps being yanked away. Detachment alone never builds the habit. Together they work like two oars. Verse thirty-six closes it: yoga is hard for the one who doesn't hold themselves, but for the one who keeps striving by the right means, it can be reached. The mind is restless. True. And not the end of the story.
screen: `THE SELF IN ALL BEINGS.` · `AS HARD AS HOLDING THE WIND.` · `KRISHNA AGREES.` · `PRACTICE AND DETACHMENT.` · then, large: `TWO OARS.`

segments.voice: Rest on one thing, the breath at the nose, and come back to it each time the mind runs off, as it will. Notice where it ran; don't chase the thought or argue with it, just let the pull fade a little. Pull on both oars: return, and let go.

Abhyasa. Practice, repeated effort, paired with vairagya, detachment. Arjuna's honest complaint, Gita six, thirty-four: the mind is restless, turbulent, strong and stubborn. Krishna agrees: by practice and detachment it can be held.
Your line: practice and detachment. Every wandering is one more stroke of the oar. That's one hundred eighty-one.

182.title: The one who fell short (6.37–6.47)
182.hook: Arjuna asks the question under every new habit: what if I start, and fail?
182.howItsDone: Gita 6.40 is often quoted by Hindu teachers to encourage people who have lapsed in practice; some commentators divide the Gita into three sets of six chapters, and chapter six closes the first.

segments.voice: Yesterday, abhyasa: Arjuna admitted the mind is restless, and Krishna agreed, and gave two oars, practice and detachment. Today, the end of the week, and the end of chapter six.

What about the person who starts with real faith, and can't keep it up? The mind wanders off, and they never get there. Do they lose both worlds? Are they like a small cloud, torn off from the big one, that just thins out and disappears? That's Arjuna's question, the one anyone asks on day nine of a new habit. And after this week, it's fair. Six days, six big asks: the city of nine gates, seated within; the sage's peace; lift yourself by yourself; how to sit; the lamp in a windless place; the restless mind. That's a lot to live up to.
screen: `WHAT IF I START, AND FAIL?` → `A CLOUD, TORN OFF AND GONE?` → `A WEEK TO LIVE UP TO.`

segments.voice: It's a painful picture, the torn cloud. You left the ordinary life, you didn't reach the spiritual one, and now you're neither. Krishna's answer is gentle. Verse forty: there is no destruction for them, Arjuna, neither here nor in the next world. No one who does good, my friend, ever comes to a bad end. The word he uses there, tata, is tender, the way an elder speaks to a child. Then he tells what happens. The one who fell short reaches the worlds of the good, and stays long. Then they're born again into a good and prosperous home, or, rarer, into a family of wise yogis. There, verse forty-three says, they get back the understanding they had before, and they strive again, harder. Verse forty-four: they're carried forward by their earlier practice, even without meaning to be. Every sit, every returned thought, every day of practice counts, and it carries. Through many lifetimes of effort, the yogi comes to the goal. The chapter ends by lifting the yogi above ascetics, scholars and ritual-doers, and saying that of all yogis, the one who turns to Krishna with faith, the inner self absorbed in him, is the closest. With that, the first six chapters of the Gita close; some commentators treat them as one unit, about action and the self. Nothing is lost.
screen: `THE TORN CLOUD.` · `NO ONE WHO DOES GOOD IS LOST.` · `THEY PICK UP WHERE THEY LEFT OFF.` · `EARLIER PRACTICE CARRIES THEM.` · then, large: `NOTHING IS LOST.`

segments.voice: Look back over this week, or this whole path so far, to a day you skipped or a sit that was all wandering, and instead of counting it against yourself, picture it the way verse forty-four does: as momentum. Every minute you did sit is still moving you. Breathe in and feel it carrying you; breathe out and let the missed days go.
Tata. My dear: the tender word Krishna uses for Arjuna. Gita six, forty: the one who strives and doesn't arrive isn't lost; earlier practice carries them forward.
Your line: nothing is lost. What you practiced is still moving you. That's chapter six, finished.
